hook.text: Galaxies didn't always exist. The first ones formed just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

buildup.text: Dark matter clumped first, creating gravitational wells. Gas fell in, ignited stars, and galaxies were born.

discovery.text: JWST found galaxies from just 300 million years after the Big Bang—far earlier than anyone expected.

twist.text: These early galaxies were surprisingly bright and massive. Current models struggle to explain how they formed so fast.

climax.text: Understanding the first galaxies may require rethinking how dark matter and gas interacted in the early cosmos.

punchline.text: Galaxies appeared shockingly early. The universe built fast.

quiz.question: What surprised astronomers about the earliest galaxies found by JWST?
options: They were far more massive and bright than models predicted for that early era
They contained no stars at all—only dark matter
They were much smaller and dimmer than expected

details.summary: The first galaxies assembled within 200-500 million years after the Big Bang from mergers of smaller star-forming clumps. JWST has revealed unexpectedly bright, mature-looking galaxies already present when the universe was less than 500 million years old — challenging models of galaxy formation.
details.whyItMatters: The first galaxies mark the transition from isolated star formation to the structured universe we see today. JWST's surprising discoveries are rewriting our understanding of how quickly galaxies can form and evolve.
takeaways: First galaxies formed within 200-500 million years after the Big Bang
They assembled from mergers of smaller star-forming clumps
JWST found unexpectedly mature galaxies challenging our models

faq.question: Why are JWST's early galaxy discoveries surprising?
faq.answer: JWST found galaxies that appear too large, too bright, and too evolved for their young age. Standard models predicted small, faint, irregular first galaxies.

faq.question: How do first galaxies differ from modern ones?
faq.answer: First galaxies were much smaller, more irregular, and forming stars at prodigious rates. They lacked the spiral and elliptical shapes of modern galaxies, contained almost no heavy elements, and were merging frequently.
